title: Spineward
concept: Your urchin is a domed shell with six sockets and nothing else. A spine plugged into a socket is a leg, an arm and a shield all at once — but only in the one direction it points — and every socket holding a spine is a socket that cannot hold a pearl, so mobility, reach, defence and cargo are literally competing for the same six holes. A turn is two actions — three if the outgoing tide runs with you — out of growing a spine, shedding one, rotating the whole shell a sixth of a turn, creeping, reaching for a pearl, robbing a neighbour who has no spine turned your way, or casting your load ashore; and casting a pearl ashore is the only moment anyone learns what it was worth, because a pearl's value is cast on the flat foot of its shaft and that foot is buried in a socket everywhere else in the game. Because landing is everywhere and the tide speeds the chaser, an urchin that banks first never simply coasts: a crown in reach is a crown in danger.
novelty: One physical part, the spine, is simultaneously the piece's movement vector, its reach, its defence and the thing occupying its cargo space — a fully-armed urchin cannot carry anything and a fully-laden one cannot move or defend itself, and both facts are visible across the table as a count of quills versus knobs. Paired with it: a value marking cast on the one face that points downward into a socket in every position the game ever puts the piece in, so pearls are opaque on the reef, opaque in a shell and opaque when robbed, and become numbers only when planted foot-up in a rack. Searches run (queries from prior_art_search.sh, all through WebSearch): the mechanism verbatim ('board game where you plug spines into sockets on your own piece and each spine is both a direction it can move and the direction it is shielded from'), the cargo half as its own product pitch ('board game piece with sockets holding either movement parts or treasure, carrying treasure reduces your movement modular pawn'), the theme+mechanism combination ('sea urchin reef board game grow spines hexagonal pans collect pearls hidden value abstract strategy'), and the plain title ('"Spineward" board game BGG'). Closest SHIPPED comparable, and it is close on exactly one half: Ploy (3M bookshelf series, 1970, BGG 1591) — pieces carry embossed direction lines, movement is restricted to those lines, and rotating a piece is itself a move. But Ploy's lines are moulded into four fixed classes (Shield/Probe/Lance/Commander), a player never adds or removes one, the lines have no defensive function whatsoever (Wikipedia's rules summary mentions none), and there is no cargo, no capacity and no hidden value — the whole 'a direction you own is a direction you gave up carrying capacity for' trade does not exist there. Pirateer (1978) turned up as a genuine but narrow partial match on the OTHER half: a ship that takes the treasure has its movement restricted while carrying it — but that is a flat rule applied to a fixed pawn, not a shared socket budget the player allocates, and Pirateer's treasure has one public value. The reef searches returned Reef (Plan B), Reef Encounter (Breese) and Reefscape, all coral-growth tile/card games with no piece-mounted parts; treat them as clean. The title returned no game of any kind — the nearest hits were 'Spinball' and the publisher Spin Master, neither of which the compound reads as.

art_direction.form_language: Wave-worn reef limestone and living shell. The board is a thick slab of rock cut into hexagonal tide pans with rounded, water-smoothed rims and a soft chamfered skirt; the urchins are heavy domed carapaces scored with deep radial grooves; the spines are stout tapered quills with blunt wedge tips, closer to a limpet's tooth than to a needle, never more than about twice as tall as they are thick. Everything is chunky and softened — 3mm minimum wall, no filigree, no spike thin enough to snap off or to hurt a hand rummaging in the box.
art_direction.silhouette: A low grey slab of rock pans with four spiny domes creeping across it, a scatter of knobbed pearls standing in the pools, and four barnacled racks along the table edge — a tidepool at dead low water, seen from standing height.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: reef_board is the only slab and the only part with hexagonal pans; nothing else has a flat top you could set a piece on. urchin_shell is the only domed hexagon — a ring of six sockets around a central grip knob whose prism carries three, four, five or six flats, and that flat count is a player's identity for the whole game, read by counting edges and never by colour. spine is the only piece with a blade: a stout upright quill with a wedge tip, unmistakable from a pearl both in silhouette and in the hand, and deliberately kept inside the shell's own footprint so it points at a neighbouring pan without ever reaching into it. The three pearl families are the only pieces with a smooth domed knob on a plain round shaft, and they are IDENTICAL to each other everywhere a player can see — the grade lives entirely on the flat foot of the shaft, which is what makes a pearl carryable in secret. pearl_rack is the only long low part, a barnacled bar of six round wells with a different end-finial prism per seat matching the shell knobs, and tide_pot is the only tall vessel, a deep blind drum with an open scalloped supply tray around its foot.
art_direction.surface_treatment: 1.2mm-deep radial grooves fan across every urchin_shell dome between its sockets, so a bare shell still reads as a living test rather than a hex nut; 1.2mm concentric ripple relief across every pan floor; a 1.2mm raised collar rings the nineteen inner seed pans and a 1.5mm raised barnacle cluster marks the six corner landing shelves, so the two special pan types are told apart by relief height as well as by pattern; 1.2mm raised concentric rings — one, two or three — on each pearl's flat foot, the only marking in the entire game that carries a number; 1.2mm barnacle stipple on the pearl_rack skirt and the tide_pot body.
art_direction.hero_shot: Low three-quarter across the reef: one urchin mid-creep with three quills out and three sockets plugged with pearl knobs, an enemy urchin a single pan away with one lone spine turned to face it, and in the foreground a rack holding four landed pearls stood foot-up, their one-, two- and three-ring feet the only numbers anywhere in the picture.

components.name: reef_board
components.desc: Hexagonal limestone slab, ~238mm across the flats, ~14mm thick with a rounded water-worn skirt. 37 hexagonal tide pans on a triangular lattice at 34mm pitch — centre pan, ring of 6, ring of 12, ring of 18 — each pan a ~30mm-across-flats, 3mm-deep dish with 1.2mm ripple relief on its floor and a 6.6mm-diameter, 10mm-deep socket at its exact centre for a pearl shaft. The pan walls index a hexagonal urchin base to one of six orientations with ~0.5mm clearance per side. The 19 inner pans (centre plus the first two rings) carry a 1.2mm raised collar and are the SEED PANS; the 6 corner pans of the outer ring carry a 1.5mm raised barnacle cluster and are the ANCHORAGES, the reef's six historic landing shelves; every pan will beach a pearl (see LAND). Fits the P2S bed in one piece.

components.name: urchin_shell
components.desc: Domed hexagonal carapace, ~29mm across the flats and ~18mm tall, with 1.2mm radial grooves fanning over the dome. Six sockets, 6.6mm diameter and 12mm deep, sunk vertically at the six face centres on a ~11mm radius — deep enough that spines and pearls stay put when the shell is lifted upright. A central grip knob 12mm across rises ~16mm for lifting and rotating. The four shells are identical apart from that knob's prism, which has three, four, five or six flats; a player's shell and their matching pearl_rack finial are their mark for the whole game. Nothing on the shell may overhang its own 29mm footprint, so a shell never fouls anything on a neighbouring pan.

components.name: spine
components.desc: The common supply of quills — exactly six per seat at a full table, so spines themselves are a contested resource. A 6mm peg 12mm long carrying a stout upright quill above it: a tapered blade ~11mm thick and ~13mm long with a blunt wedge tip, standing ~20mm proud of the shell, chunky enough to pinch out and never a needle. Seated in a socket it points squarely at one neighbouring pan and stays wholly inside the shell's footprint.

components.name: pearl_one_ring
components.desc: The common grade. A smooth domed knob ~16mm across and ~11mm tall on a plain round 6mm shaft ~16mm long. Above the shaft it is indistinguishable from every other pearl in the game; the only marking is on the flat foot of the shaft — a single 1.2mm raised ring — and that foot faces down into a socket in every pan and every shell, so it can only be read once the pearl is stood foot-up in a rack.

components.name: pearl_two_ring
components.desc: The middle grade. Identical to pearl_one_ring in every visible respect; two concentric 1.2mm raised rings on the foot.

components.name: pearl_three_ring
components.desc: The rare grade. Identical to pearl_one_ring in every visible respect; three concentric 1.2mm raised rings on the foot.

components.name: pearl_rack
components.desc: Landing rack, ~135 x 34 x 22mm, barnacle-stippled skirt, with six round wells 17mm across and 9mm deep in a row, each with a thumb scallop, holding a pearl knob-down so its ringed foot stands ~16mm proud and readable across the table. One end carries a triangular, square, pentagonal or hexagonal prism finial matching that seat's shell knob. Six wells is a hard capacity.

components.name: tide_pot
components.desc: The supply vessel: a deep blind drum ~85mm across and ~95mm tall whose mouth a palm can cover, used at setup to shake and blind-draw the pearls so nobody sees a foot, with an open scalloped tray ~150mm across moulded around its foot that holds the spine supply in the open where every seat can reach it. Barnacle stipple, 1.2mm, on the drum.

setup.text: Set the reef_board in the middle of the table. It has 37 hexagonal pans. The 19 inner pans (the centre pan and the first two rings around it) are ringed with a raised collar: those are the SEED PANS. The 6 corner pans of the outer ring carry a raised barnacle cluster: those are the ANCHORAGES, the reef's six historic landing shelves; the whole coast takes a landing too (see LAND). Every pan, of every kind, has a socket at its centre that a pearl can stand in.

Drop all 16 pearls into the deep drum of the tide_pot, cover its mouth with your palm and shake. A pearl's grade is one, two or three raised rings on the flat FOOT of its shaft, and that foot points down into a socket everywhere the game will ever put it — so from this moment nobody knows what any pearl on the reef is worth.

Going clockwise from any player, each in turn reaches into the tide_pot without looking, draws one pearl and stands it shaft-down in any empty seed pan, never turning it over. Repeat until all 16 pearls are planted; three seed pans will be left bare.
Tip all 24 spines into the open tray around the tide_pot's foot. That is the common supply for the whole game — six per seat at a full table and no more, so spines can genuinely run short.

Each player takes one urchin_shell — the grip knobs have three, four, five and six flats, and the one you take is your mark for the game — and the pearl_rack whose end finial has the same number of flats, which stands in front of their seat, empty.

Choose a first player any way you like; play passes clockwise. In turn order each player stands their urchin_shell on any empty pan of the OUTER ring that is not a landing shelf and is not next to another urchin. Then, in REVERSE turn order, each player takes two spines from the supply and stands one in each of two sockets of their own shell, in whichever two directions they like.

turn.text: WHAT A SPINE IS (the fact the whole game runs on). Your shell has six sockets, one facing each of the six sides of the pan it stands in. A spine standing in a socket is a leg, an arm and a shield at the same time — but only towards the one neighbouring pan it points at. Every single thing you do in a direction needs a spine already pointing that way. A socket holding a pearl is a socket doing none of that, and an empty socket is doing none of it either. Six sockets is your entire budget for movement, reach, defence and cargo together.

On your turn you take actions from the list below — TWO of them, or THREE if you are riding the tide (THE TIDE, the last entry). You may take the same action more than once. Then play passes clockwise.

THE TIDE — the catch-up that keeps a lead from ever being a foregone conclusion. At the START of each of your turns, add the ringed feet showing in every pearl_rack. If your own total is strictly below the table's highest banked total, the outgoing current runs with you: you take THREE actions this turn; otherwise you take the usual two. The count is public — everyone reads who is riding the tide and who is paying for the lead straight off the racks. This is why there is no coasting to a crown: a leader acts fewer times than a chaser, and to hold a lead must keep banking while doing less, while a chaser can always bank harder — or rob the leader's carried load before it is cast ashore.
GROW. Take one spine from the supply tray and stand it in an empty socket of your shell. If the tray is empty you cannot grow.
SHED. Pull one spine out of your shell and return it to the supply tray, freeing that socket.

TURN. Lift your shell straight up and set it back in the same pan rotated one step — a sixth of a turn — either way. Every spine and every pearl in it turns with it, so this re-aims your whole rosette at once. Sockets are deep enough that nothing falls out; do not tip the shell over.

CREEP. Move your shell into a neighbouring pan you have a spine pointing at. The pan must be genuinely empty: a pan holding another urchin or a standing pearl cannot be entered, so pearls are obstacles as well as prizes. Your shell keeps its facing.

TAKE. Lift a pearl out of a neighbouring pan you have a spine pointing at, and drop it straight into an empty socket of your shell without turning it over. You do not look at its foot and nor does anyone else — you are carrying an unknown weight, and so is everybody else.

ROB. Legal only when all five are true: an enemy urchin stands in a neighbouring pan, you have a spine pointing at it, that urchin has NO spine pointing back at you, you have an empty socket, and that enemy is carrying at least one pearl in its sockets. If the enemy is carrying no pearl, ROB simply is not offered as a move — it costs you nothing, but it does nothing either. Otherwise, take any one pearl from its sockets — they are identical from above, so you are choosing blind — and drop it into your empty socket. A spine turned to face a threat is the only defence in the game, and it costs you the socket it stands in.

LAND. Legal from any pan — you pass a carried pearl to the outgoing tide, which beaches it into an empty well of your pearl_rack. As you cast it, turn it over so its ringed foot stands foot-up, revealing its grade — this is the only moment in the game a pearl's grade is ever seen, by you or by anyone. You may land as many carried pearls as you like up to the empty wells you have; your rack holds six and no more, and pearls that do not fit stay in your sockets. (The six corner pans of the outer ring are the reef's historic landing shelves, its deep anchorages, but the tide will beach a pearl anywhere it is cast.)

TWO THINGS THAT FOLLOW, and nobody has to be told them twice: an urchin with six spines can go anywhere and cannot be robbed, and can carry nothing at all; an urchin with six pearls cannot move, cannot reach, cannot defend itself and cannot even shed, because shedding needs a spine to shed. Both extremes score nothing. The game is the middle.

end.text: The game ends as normal when either trigger fires: no pearl is left standing anywhere on the reef_board, or any pearl_rack holds six pearls; either way finish the round so that every player has taken the same number of turns, then stop. The CROWN (rules:win) is an exception and overrides both triggers: the instant a player's rack total reaches the crown value, the game ends on the spot with that player as the sole winner, before the round finishes.

It also ends if FOUR full rounds go by in a row in which no pearl is LANDED in a rack by anybody — the reef has gone slack. Taking, dropping and robbing are churn, not progress: the crown only advances when a pearl is banked, so a table that keeps shuffling pearls around without banking one is as stuck as a table sitting still. A single landing anywhere resets the count. This clause is a backstop and deliberately generous so a long chase can develop before it fires; it exists because a crown cannot come to a table that has stopped producing landings.

win.text: THE CROWN. A pearl_rack's total is public from the moment its first pearl is landed, because the ringed feet stand foot-up as numbers the whole table can read. The FIRST player whose rack total reaches the crown value wins the game immediately, as a sole winner — the round is not finished, because a crown cannot be shared. The crown value is 6 at every player count. Six is bankable even on a crowded, robbing four-player reef because the tide beaches a pearl from anywhere — no long dock pilgrimage to a single shelf is needed — and at two players it is a straight, reachable race again. And six is long enough, and the race late enough, that the tide's catch-up (rules:turn[THE TIDE]) gets to decide it: a leader cannot simply bank first and coast, because the chaser is always acting more often and can rob the leader's carried load before it is cast ashore. A crown in reach is a crown in danger — that is the comeback that keeps a decided game close. If the game ends without a crown — the reef emptied, a rack reached six, or four silent rounds — the best haul wins: add the feet in your rack, a one-ring scoring 1, a two-ring 2, a three-ring 3, and pearls still riding in your shell's sockets score nothing at all. Highest total wins. If two or more are level, the tied player who landed the most pearls wins; if still level, the tied player carrying the fewest pearls in their shell wins (unlanded pearls are worth nothing, so among equals holding the least dead weight played better); if still level, the tied player with the most spines standing in their shell; if that ties too, they share the win.
